standard.title: Graphing Linear Relations and Solving Equations
standard.description: graph linear relations on the Cartesian plane using digital tools where appropriate; solve linear equations and one-variable inequalities using graphical and algebraic techniques; verify solutions by substitution
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can plot ordered pairs and describe linear relationships on the Cartesian plane (from AC9M7A05). Students can solve one-variable linear equations (from AC9M7A03).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students graph linear relations including inequalities, solve linear equations algebraically and graphically, and verify solutions by substitution.

nodes.label: Graphing linear relations including inequalities
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students graph linear relations of the form y = mx + b and one-variable inequalities on the Cartesian plane, identifying key features.
nodes.minimum_width: Graph a linear relation y = mx + b from a table of values and identify gradient and y-intercept.
nodes.typical_width: Graph linear relations and inequalities (x = a, y = a, y ≤ mx + b); identify gradient and intercepts; describe the effect of changing m and b.
wider: Investigate what happens to the graph when m is negative, zero, or undefined — connect each case to a physical or real-world interpretation.
Explore graphing two linear relations on the same axes and identifying the point of intersection — preview of simultaneous equations.

response_modes.reason: Students who only graph y = mx + b forms often fail with x = a or inequality forms. Exposure to the full range of linear relation types prevents incomplete understanding.

nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires graphical verification of inequality solutions — students who have not worked with inequality graph forms (including boundary line conventions) cannot use graphical methods to verify their algebraic solutions.
success_criteria: Correctly graphs a linear relation from a rule or table.
Identifies gradient and y-intercept from graph and equation.
Correctly represents an inequality including the boundary line convention (solid vs dashed).

nodes.label: Solving linear equations algebraically
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students solve linear equations of the form ax + b = cx + d algebraically, including equations requiring expansion, and verify by substitution.
nodes.minimum_width: Solve a two-step linear equation with the unknown on both sides (e.g. 3x + 7 = 6x − 9).
nodes.typical_width: Solve linear equations requiring expansion of brackets; solve equations involving fractions; always verify by substitution.
wider: Solve linear equations arising from geometry problems: find the value of x given angle relationships or perimeter conditions.
Investigate equations with no solution or infinitely many solutions — what do these look like graphically?

response_modes.reason: Solving equations with unknowns on both sides requires procedural fluency and reliable sign handling. This is a high-error-rate skill that needs sustained practice before graphical methods are layered on.

nodes.hinge_reason: Equation-solving fluency and sign handling are directly required in Node 3 inequality solving — students who make systematic sign errors in equations will apply the same errors in inequalities, including failure to reverse the inequality sign when required.
success_criteria: Solves a linear equation with unknowns on both sides correctly.
Does not leave the unknown on both sides after the first step.

nodes.label: Solving inequalities and using graphical methods
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students solve one-variable inequalities algebraically and verify using graphical methods; represent solutions on a number line.
nodes.minimum_width: Solve a one-variable inequality of the form ax + b < c and represent the solution on a number line.
nodes.typical_width: Solve inequalities algebraically including those requiring reversal of the inequality sign when dividing by a negative; represent on number line and verify graphically.
wider: Investigate why dividing by a negative reverses the inequality — use a number line argument to justify.
Explore compound inequalities (a < x < b) and represent their solution sets on a number line.

response_modes.reason: Inequality solving requires a specific reasoning scaffold around sign reversal — students need an explicit rule and a conceptual justification or they apply it inconsistently.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The justification for inequality reversal when multiplying/dividing by a negative is a rich reasoning task — advancing students who can construct a number line argument are developing genuine algebraic proof reasoning.
success_criteria: Solves a one-variable inequality correctly including sign reversal where needed.
Represents the solution on a number line with correct open/closed endpoint.
Verifies the solution graphically or by substitution.
